- If sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peak values by 2–5%.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and prices are trending down, model often underestimates the drop; adjust downward by 3–7% to match true decline.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > 75.0), model frequently overcorrects or overshoots; cap forecast at +3–5% above peak or apply mean-reversion to prior 5-day average.
- When sentiment swings sharply (e.g., 0.33 → 1.00 or vice versa), model reacts with lag; delay peak forecast by 1–2 days or reduce magnitude of sudden moves.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion toward 70–72 range after 75+ peaks, model overestimates continuation; apply downward bias of 1–3% for 3–5 days post-spike.
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is neutral (0.33–0.67) and history shows low volatility, model tends to over-smooth; add 1–2% noise or slight upward bias to avoid underprediction.
- If sentiment history shows repeated 0.00 or 1.00 extremes, model often fails to capture sentiment reversal; use sentiment-weighted moving average to dampen extreme forecasts.
